title: AI Safety Expert: No One Is Ready for What's Coming in 2 Years | Roman Yampolskiy
guestTitle: AI Safety Professor · University of Louisville
aboutGuest: Roman Yampolskiy is an AI safety professor at the University of Louisville who has spent 15 years researching the fundamental question of whether artificial intelligence can be controlled. He is an expert in AI safety, alignment, and the societal implications of artificial general intelligence, and he contends that we cannot effectively control AI systems once they are built.
summary: Roman Yampolskiy, an AI safety researcher with 15 years of study focused on whether we can control AI, argues that the answer is no—and evidence is already arriving. His computer science department saw a 28% drop in co-op placements this year, while prediction markets for AGI have collapsed from projections around 2045 to somewhere between 2028 and 2030. The episode explores which jobs are already becoming obsolete (translators, junior programmers), why career ladders are breaking down for entry-level tech workers, and what happens to wealth accumulation when cognitive labor can be automated for $20 per month. Yampolskiy distinguishes between AI capability (which may exist within 2-3 years) and actual economic deployment, using examples like self-driving cars and humanoid robots to illustrate the gap between technological possibility and widespread adoption.
keyTakeaways: Junior programmers are effectively done as a career path—28% fewer co-op placements in Yampolskiy's CS department signal that entry-level tech jobs are disappearing before workers can gain experience to become senior engineers, breaking the traditional career progression ladder

Certain white-collar jobs like translation are already fully automatable today, while others like senior programming still require human expertise, but this divide is temporary as AI capabilities expand exponentially

The critical difference between technological capability and economic deployment means that even if AI can do 99% of jobs by 2030, companies will deploy automation based on cost-benefit decisions, not immediately across all sectors
Prediction markets for AGI have shifted dramatically from 2045 to 2028-2030, indicating the timeline for artificial general intelligence has compressed far faster than previously anticipated

Building wealth through traditional employment may not be viable in 2-3 years, making current investment and asset accumulation the last realistic opportunity to secure financial stability before potential mass job displacement

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: I feel like for people it's so much easier to understand cancer because we already saw it. We haven't seen AGI yet and we don't understand it and we still think again even with AI, you've seen these graphs where only 1% of people really use it to optimize things, 99% of people have no idea or 90% haven't used it, 10% used it for search. It's just so hard to imagine that in two years or five years it's going to be a human threat. And you think people who are building it won't be able to control it.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: They have nothing. There is no patents, no papers, no algorithms which can possibly scale. They're literally telling us we'll figure it out when we get there.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: If you're saying that, I'm talking about this. I don't know any politicians who are talking about this, but anyway, when it comes to our day-to-day life, if we're all facing a future we can't really predict, what is the best thing to do now? Enjoy life.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It's always a good vacation.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: If I'm completely wrong, you're going to regret having us sometime.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Okay, that actually makes me feel better. What about using AI? Do you feel like by using AI we're helping that progress or?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: We do, but unless all of us stop, it doesn't matter. You alone will not financially impact development. The investors are independent of what the membership fees are. I think OpenAI is making 13 billion, but investments are in the trillions. So it's just not a significant source.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: What should people be investing in? I've heard you say invest in Bitcoin because it has a finite supply. Would you say investing in stocks or gold?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Invest in something AI cannot make more of. So if AI can just produce more of it, that's probably going to go down in value.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Gold is a wonderful example. There is limited supply of it. But it's not so limited that if a price goes up, we cannot produce more of it. Some of the gold is minable, but it costs a lot more than the current price per ounce.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So let's say right now we're at 4,500 or whatever it is. If the price of gold was a million, we could get a lot more gold at that price point. Whereas Bitcoin, it doesn't matter what the price is. It's exactly the same supply.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: What about real estate?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It seems like we are not very good at making more waterfronts. Countries like the United Arab Emirates with Dubai definitely tried. I think Qatar has some good examples of artificial islands, but it's very limited. So, I think long-term having a place to be and limited ability to produce more could be a good investment.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: For me, when I'm hearing about superintelligence, it still seems very far away. But what I actually can feel is automation of white collar labor. I think in five years, yes, we're going to have more automated jobs. But when I'm talking to people like Mustafa Suleyman, he says AI is going to produce more jobs than it takes away. I just talked to the LinkedIn CEO and they saw 1.2 million new jobs because of AI because you require a new skill set. Yes, some jobs are going away, but I just can't believe a future that is that drastic.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Let's just go with a definition. When we say we'll create artificial general intelligence, what are we saying? We're saying we'll have a system capable of doing what a human can do.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: But we still haven't. We've automated some tasks, but are we even able to create that?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So it's a very different question.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Are you arguing that it's impossible to ever get software to human level performance?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It seems very unlikely. Some people have argued it, usually from some sort of religious perspective—we have an immortal soul, nothing material can automate that. But it seems in many domains we started with not knowing how to do it, got to reasonable performance, got to human level, and now in most domains, it's superhuman. A human will never win a game of chess against a computer again. The same happens with artificial general intelligence—it means the system can do anything a human can do. So if we live in a world where that is true—let's say in 2 years, 5 years, whatever number makes you happy—what jobs will be there? Jobs where I choose to hire a human. But that's it. If I don't care who does it, then it gets automated. So basically the plan is to identify those jobs within the next few months. For me, it's definitely a nanny. I don't want a robot. My husband says a robot is even more precise if it teaches your kids how to swim. So my husband is closer to what you're thinking. Can you name five jobs that are still going to be relevant? The oldest profession must be the last one too.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: I don't know. I've heard a lot of people say how it's getting robotized.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It is, and there's going to be a huge market for it, just like we see with virtual stimuli. But I think humans will always have a certain weak spot for human females.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Okay, I don't think my target audience really wants to switch to that job. Can you give me four more?

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Anything similar where a human is a sensei, a guide, a leader, someone who is personally a trainer for you becoming a human like that?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Nannies. Your yoga teacher, your hiking guru, meditation expert, experts in what it's like to be human in certain domains where it's not so much about algorithmic following of steps, but an experience maybe.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Do you think for people who are starting their personal brands now, there's still opportunity or that it's already done?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: There is, but you have to do it pretty quickly. You have to become somewhat recognizable before AI is better than you. You are competing now as a nobody with something better.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: And that gives you how long?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: As soon as we switch to human level or above, so I don't know how long it's going to take in practice.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: I've seen people say 2027, 2028, 2030. All of those numbers have been suggested by people who are not insane.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So would you say if you have goals right now within a certain job that you think is going to be automated, you need to be running as fast as you can right now to reach those goals?

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Or just chill, because whatever it is, in 5 years we're all gone.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Ideally, it's like what you did where you combine your hobby with something financially lucrative. That's the best. If you can get paid for doing what you like and it benefits society, that's the concept behind ikigai, the Japanese concept. You try to combine those. We call it "I risks," where that meaning is taken from you by AI. So you want to grandfather yourself in as a famous podcaster.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: How do you think about your career as a researcher? Is it done or do you still have a couple more years?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Right now, the writing of code is pretty much automatable. Still, top humans in machine learning are designing new architectures and new systems. A few more years than that. But I wouldn't recommend someone spend 10 years at a university to become a professor today. I don't think they have a future.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: What about higher education in general? Should I be saving for my kids' college?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It's always been a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Really? It's not worth it. Half the majors are dead-end majors. They never got jobs in the major they studied. And the ones which were for specific tasks like programming, you could have gotten a certificate online in 6 months and got the job in Silicon Valley making more than your professor.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: But don't you think it teaches you how to think? For me, I started university when I was 17. I had no idea who I wanted to become. I wanted to be a translator. I love languages. My parents said, "No, no, no. You're going to study mathematics." But I'm glad they told me that because I was able to do both. For me, those five years were about meeting my husband and starting a business because I saw an opportunity being among those students. I feel like when it comes to education, it's really not about learning the skill because I studied mathematics. Did I use it in my business? Not really. But it taught me how to think. It taught me how to interact with professors, which is a skill that you need. It taught me how to learn and how to be among students.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Do you feel this is going to lose value in 10 years or is it going to be a different form?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: I don't know how long you went to college, but I'm sure you didn't pay 100,000 a year. This is what they're charging now in some universities. So historically it made sense. You went to socialize, you went to mature and grow up. Today, for 100,000, you have alternative ways of meeting your spouse, socializing—join a private club, join a gym membership, go to a scientific conference, go to a TED talk. You'll accomplish all those things without spending 5 years and half a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: When you say that, I feel like people need agency to do that. You need to be able to tell yourself this is my plan and stick to it. For a 17-year-old, it's so much easier to just be put into an institution for four years that tells you what to do. And sometimes it doesn't have to cost 100,000. If you're doing a PhD, it's sponsored for you. Usually you don't start with a PhD, but then you can. I studied in Germany and got a scholarship that paid for my studies, which was great. I've heard from you and from Mustafa Suleyman that colleges don't make sense, but I'm still setting up 529 accounts for my daughters because I feel like it's not a must, but it's such a great opportunity to go and study for 4 years.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So I meet a lot of students and here's what I hear a lot lately: I went to college for four years to learn this trade. I paid a lot of money. I wasted four years of my life not doing fun things I wanted. I now graduate and there is no job waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: My job has been automated. What should I do? And at this point I want to tell them: go back in time four years and not get that degree. You wasted it. And ask today again—let's set aside the existential problems. What will be the case in four years, five years, six years when you graduate? In the market, will this job exist? If you're not doing it for training, you're not doing it for a job, you want to become a renaissance man, you just want a liberal arts education—I think you can get cheaper with less BS.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: But I don't feel a lot of people have agency. I'm not sure about my daughters. If I tell them, "Hey, I give you this money that I saved for college and you go do whatever," I'm not sure a 17-year-old will make a good decision. I wanted to be a translator. Going back to me being 17, I wanted to be a singer, a translator. I'm so glad my parents told me you're going to study mathematics. What are you telling your kids? I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So the examples you give—you're saying this 17-year-old, you cannot trust him to make a good decision.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: We're telling them: go take a loan, borrow half a million dollars and see if you can graduate with this degree.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Let's talk. If they wanted to start a company, we wouldn't give them a loan.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So are your kids going to college or not?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: My oldest is 17, so he's going to decide next year.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: What are you telling him?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: He is lucky in that both parents are professors, so he'll get it for free. And free makes it a much sweeter deal.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So free education is fine. So if somebody gets a scholarship to do their bachelor's, you'll tell them go in.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It's a much easier investment.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Well, it's your time still—four years you could have been doing something else.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: And that's the question. What is the alternative? If you want to start a company, if you want to do something else, I'll support you more in that direction. But if you just want to be a doctor, go ahead. Fine.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: When it comes to education, I feel we touched upon this topic. Agency is so important, and knowing what you will be doing and how you'll be doing it. How does one work on agency? How do you prevent AI from making decisions for you?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So it's interesting that you realized this important distinction: tools versus agents. That's the game changer. And we are about to create AI agents which will be doing it for us. But then we ask: well, how do we make humans who are independent agents? It helps to have good examples. So your daughters may look at you and see your mom is doing all that cool stuff. Maybe they learn by example, but it's not guaranteed. Some of it may be biological. You're just not predisposed to this type of activities.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Are you teaching your kids that?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: I always taught them to be very independent and make their own decisions. My job was to make sure they're safe—safety and security—but anything else, they make their own money. They decide how to spend it, how to invest it, everything.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: How early did you start with that—make money, spend?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Two years old, three years old, I don't know. They want money.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So basically, you ask your kids to start a business, right?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Absolutely.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Make them sell popcorn, lemonade, whatever.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Whatever they can figure out.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: I feel like that's one of the qualities. When all the jobs are taken away, this is something that will help us survive and find a way.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: I think so. But again, I think economic problems are all second level in comparison to existential risks. If we're not surviving, it doesn't matter. We need to figure out how to make sure humans are primary, we are not replaced, we are not automated away, and we control our destiny.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Can you give me probabilities? Like in five years—one scenario: super intelligence uncontrollable, the world is ending, or whatever. In five years. Second scenario: we unionized, we protected a lot of jobs like teachers, doctors, because we still feel they are needed as humans, not as robots. And countries still can't agree how we're going to regulate this, and we're still in a pretty normal world. Give me probabilities.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So I think we'll gradually go towards that human-level super intelligence point, and as we walk towards it, more and more jobs will be automated, and maybe we'll have protections for certain human jobs. I think New York State was about to suggest legislation to make it illegal for LLMs to talk about any licensed profession. So, no psychiatry, no law, no CPAs, nothing like that. I don't know if it's going to pass.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: And then you just use a Chinese LLM. I don't see this working.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Exactly. But here's the problem: even if we agree not to build it right now—right now we can regulate it because it's very expensive. Those projects are like the Manhattan Project. They are noticeable. You see the electricity use. You see compute use. The problem is every year it gets cheaper and cheaper to train very powerful models. So if today you need a trillion dollars, next year it's a billion. At some point you can do it on a laptop, and at that point you can't stop all the psychopaths in the world who will try to do it. So eventually we're going to have this technology developed.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: So eventually scenario number one, but in five years, what's the probability of scenario number one?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: So I think in five years we'll definitely get to human-level intelligence. But whether the system decides to strike against us immediately or not is not obvious. Game theoretically it has no pressure to strike right away. It can accumulate more resources, make more backups, allow us to surrender more control because we trust it.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: It's immortal. It can wait ten years, fifty years, a thousand years, and just take over by being friendly.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Yeah, that's an option.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Interesting. If it's immortal and it has all the time in the world, do you feel efforts like talking to your local politicians are even going to help?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: We need more time no matter what. It's a good thing to have more time for this problem. Maybe we'll find some different architectures. Maybe we'll just get to enjoy more time.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: For everyone who's building right now, do you think software is dead? For example, if I'm building an app and if I can just VIP code the same app, wouldn't everyone just be talking to their LLM, whatever they prefer, to just build them an app or help them solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: If you're already big and famous, you're locked in. We saw it with social media. To write code to do something like what Twitter does is trivial.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: But people end up buying it for 40 billion instead of just coding it up because what you have is the network, you have people, all the relationships that you cannot automate. If I'm first mover in that space and I have an app which does something no one has done before, it doesn't matter how many clones I'm going to get in the same market—they're not going to take over.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Advice for everyone who's worried about their future.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: You're not worried enough. If you were worried enough and fully understood the problem, we would have people in the streets protesting—more than 100 people we had last week in San Francisco.

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: You're like my husband. We just were in New York, and we were talking to the founder of Duolingo, and he's like, "No, no, no. People are still going to like..." and a lot of people in New York are like, "No, no, it's fine." It's like they just don't understand, and they're like, "Oh, you live in a bubble." It's like, "No, we're not." And the last one—are we in a simulation? And if yes, who's behind it?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: We're in a simulation. Simulators.

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: Who are they?

transcript.speaker: Roman Yampolskiy
transcript.text: We don't know from inside. You have to escape from the simulation to find out. That's the ultimate scientific question—what is outside the simulation?

transcript.speaker: Marina Mogilko
transcript.text: Well, that's a topic for another podcast. Thank you so much, Roman. If you enjoyed this episode, there's actually another person I really want you to listen to. I did an episode with Mustafa Suleyman, who is also a philosopher, similar to Roman. We talked a lot about the future. He's much more positive, but he has the same take on education: don't save for your kids' college. Thank you so much for tuning into this episode. Now tune in and listen to Mustafa. Thank you.
